title: Eager Execution & Computational Graphs 🧠
description: Discover how TensorFlow runs code instantly vs. building static graphs.

slides.title: Two Ways to Execute 🆚
slides.content:
# Eager Execution (TF 2.x default)

Operations are evaluated **immediately** – just like normal Python. Great for debugging.

```python
x = tf.constant([1,2])
y = x + 1   # instantly computes [2,3]
print(y)   # tf.Tensor([2 3], shape=(2,), dtype=int32)
```

# Graph Execution (TF 1.x style)

First you define a **computational graph** (a blueprint), then run it in a session. More optimised but harder to debug.

quizData.question: In TensorFlow 2.x, operations are executed...
quizData.explanation: Eager execution is the default in TF 2.x, so operations run instantly.

slides.title: Eager in Action 🏃
slides.codeSnippet:
import tensorflow as tf

a = tf.constant(5.0)
b = tf.constant(3.0)
c = a * b + 2.0
print("Result:", c.numpy())   # 17.0

# You can even use Python control flow directly!
if c > 10:
    print("Greater than 10!")

slides.title: Graphs Still Matter 🗺️
slides.content: Even in eager mode, TensorFlow **traces** your code into a graph when you wrap it with `@tf.function`. This gives you the best of both worlds: easy debugging *and* high performance!

quizData.question: True or False: In eager mode, you cannot use Python if‑statements on tensors.
quizData.explanation: In eager mode, tensors behave like NumPy arrays – you can use Python control flow naturally.
